# Data and DevOps Tools for Evaluating and Productionizing LLMs (E16g)

**What it is:** A Vanishing Gradients livestream with Hamel Husain, Rechat CTO Emil, and host Hugo Bowne-Anderson. Published 2023-11-04. Duration: 1 hour 4 minutes 40 seconds. [Watch the video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B_DMMlDuJB0).

**Capture status:** Full auto-generated transcript. Caption fragments were joined without word changes. No transcript section is marked missing. Screen demonstrations are described in speech, but the capture does not contain their code, charts, or interfaces. Despite the packet filename, the captured title is not “Your AI Product Needs Evals”. Shreya and the recipe-chatbot course are not discussed.

**Caption uncertainty:** Metadata supplies “Hamel Husain”, “Rechat,” and “Lucy”. Captions vary these into “Hussain”, “Rate Chat,” “Reach Out”, “Richard,” and “Lucene”. “ML,” “Emma”, and “Amir” likely refer to Emil, but that is a guess. “LangStreet” likely means LangFree in the synthetic-data discussion, but the caption alone does not settle it. The spoken alternative tracing project, “open LLM-etry”, is uncertain. These guesses are not exact tool identifiers.

## The point in three sentences

Build an improvement loop around recorded conversations, human review, and tests for failures you actually observe. Rechat demonstrates this with Lucy, an assistant that calls functions to perform real estate tasks, using existing TypeScript infrastructure and a custom review interface. The loop produces both regression checks and curated training examples, while comparisons reveal that fixing one failure can increase another.

## Key ideas

- Start with actual product tasks and awkward scenarios. Missing listings and nonexistent contacts matter alongside successful requests. “what happens if uh there isn't a listing in the database?” [00:25:24]
- Record a trace, the sequence of prompts, model responses, function calls, and function results. The point is retaining evidence for review, regardless of the logging vendor. “you don't have to use LangSmith, use something.” [00:20:53]
- Link results to the prompts and code that produced them. Versioning means preserving which versions belong together, rather than keeping a pile of unrelated conversations. “we know what code is a tied to what prompt” [00:21:52]
- Judge the system's response to the user before assigning blame to the model or application. Blank output, malformed JSON, repeated prompt text, and exposed user IDs are examples of observed failures. “We care about what is this system saying to the user.” [00:27:33]
- Use simple assertions, code checks that detect a specific failure, wherever possible. The demonstrated checks are written in TypeScript. “These are assertions.” [00:29:08]
- The demonstrated model tests call the real API and run the application through its flow. Although initially called unit tests, the speakers accept the more accurate name, integration tests. “Those are integration tests.” [00:37:25]
- Model responses can vary between runs. Compare results across many cases rather than treating one successful response as proof. “one time you run it, it works, one other time it may fail.” [00:23:52]
- Stay with a familiar stack when it lets you reuse working infrastructure. Rechat kept TypeScript so its AI work could use existing APIs and CI, continuous integration that runs checks when code changes. “we decided to stick with the technology that we had.” [00:33:05]
- Make review fast and specific to the job. The custom interface displays conversations and function results, supports accept/reject labels, filters scenarios, and shows review progress. “you want to be able to rapidly review this data.” [00:35:52]
- Separate routing bad examples for repair from collecting good examples for training. Rechat lets reviewers edit the final response, but deliberately avoids editing intermediate steps because Hamel fears introducing mistakes. “we just want to be able to correct the output.” [00:40:02]
- Keep training conversations consistent with production prompts. Removing a formatting instruction from the live flow also requires removing it from fine-tuning data, examples used for additional model training. “You don't want things in your fine-tuning data that don't reflect real like don't reflect production.” [00:46:58]
- Synthetic requests, generated by another model, can expand the cases available for review. Existing assertions filter obvious failures before humans inspect the remaining examples. “We reused them here” [00:55:39]
- Compare all failure categories after a change. A fine-tuned model removed an invalid-placeholder problem in the shown results but increased another error. “Like you fix one thing, you might break another thing.” [01:00:19]
- Build the loop gradually and keep replacing parts as needed. Airtable and Shiny were pragmatic choices, not promises about a permanent architecture. “don't take on extreme complexity either with infrastructure or tooling.” [01:02:25]

## How to do it (concrete steps, checklists, templates)

The demonstrated sequence is:

1. Have the QA team, people testing the product, converse with Lucy and report issues. Start with human requests and actual capabilities such as creating marketing or finding listings. [00:10:02]–[00:10:32]
2. Capture the complete sequence in LangSmith. Add a developer debug link from a conversation to its trace. Record the associated code and prompts. [00:18:06]–[00:21:52]
3. Inspect the logged data. Identify concrete failures and product scenarios, then write assertions for them. Examples include blank responses, bad JSON, repetition, and exposed IDs. [00:25:16]–[00:31:11]
4. Run an offline scenario dataset through the application whenever relevant code changes. These tests still make live model API calls. Look at aggregate results. Add assertions and scenarios when new failures appear. [00:31:11], [00:37:18]–[00:37:33], [00:51:15]–[00:51:46]
5. Export trace data through LangFree into a review database. Use the Shiny interface to review full conversations, accept or reject examples, filter by scenario, and edit final outputs when appropriate. Route failures for work and retain accepted examples by feature. [00:36:10]–[00:44:45]
6. Use curated conversations for fine-tuning. Also improve prompts based on what review reveals. Version prompts and training examples together so training reflects the production flow. [00:44:45]–[00:47:14]
7. Expand coverage with GPT-4-generated requests. For the email tool, ask for 50 different requests from a real estate agent. Run these against Lucy, apply the existing assertions, collect passing examples, then have humans review them. [00:55:11]–[00:57:37]
8. Upload CI results to Postgres and compare runs in Metabase. The demonstration compares the same dataset and commit across default and fine-tuned models. Check which errors disappeared and which increased. Repeat the loop. [00:58:02]–[01:01:34]

Future steps are explicitly separate. Semantic search in the review app and editing/replaying traces are proposed additions [00:40:44], [00:45:38]. Automated grading could use a reward model, a classifier producing a quality signal, or GPT-4, with its agreement against human evaluations tracked before reducing human review [00:47:20]–[00:48:19]. A/B testing, comparing product variants with users, and live user feedback are later-stage work; reward models and RLHF, training from human feedback, are not demonstrated [00:05:50], [00:48:28]–[00:49:01].

## Numbers and strong claims

- **3880 seconds:** Duration from capture metadata, equivalent to [01:04:40].
- **“close to zero”:** Emil says LangChain's retry behavior reduced a group of function-call issues to this level [00:15:47]. Practitioner claim; no counts or denominator supplied.
- **“minutes”:** LangSmith activation reportedly took minutes [00:18:06]. Anecdotal setup claim, not a general timing guarantee.
- **50 requests, hundreds of cases:** The synthetic email script asks GPT-4 for 50 requests and can generate hundreds of cases in minutes [00:55:39]. No measured runtime or cost is given.
- **Every relevant commit:** The pipeline runs when a commit changes AI-related behavior [00:51:17]. Emil calls it cheap for Rechat [00:51:53]; Hamel warns the same setup could be too expensive elsewhere [00:52:26]–[00:52:38]. No dollar figure is supplied.
- **Targeted errors eliminated:** The speakers report invalid placeholders and empty listing-search responses disappearing in the displayed comparisons [00:59:47], [01:00:59]. This is a result for the shown runs, not proof those errors can never recur. Exact rates, sample sizes, and chart values are absent from the text. Another error increased [00:59:47].
- **Data review as the differentiator:** Hamel says successful projects differ in whether they examine their data [00:28:37]–[00:28:51]. Strong practitioner opinion, not a controlled study.

## Compared with the deep research report

The report does not mention this video directly. The comparison concerns its picture of Hamel and Shreya's method and the recipe-chatbot learning repository, not verification of that course's contents.

- **What it gets right:** The report says the field guide involves “inspecting real data, identifying failure patterns, building useful review interfaces”. This video gives a concrete Rechat example: “you want to be able to rapidly review this data.” [00:35:52] The custom interface connects review to tests, repair work, and training examples.
- **What it adds to the course picture:** The report describes Recipe Chatbot as “Primarily Python” and prioritizes failure discovery, model-based evaluation, and agent traces. This separate demonstration shows “this is TypeScript.” [00:30:26] It adds an existing-product implementation using ordinary assertions and CI. It does not establish anything about the course's code or history.
- **What the report leaves out of this example:** It says evaluation belongs in “an engineering feedback loop”. The video supplies operational details: final-output editing, feature-based curation, synthetic requests filtered through shared assertions, and prompt/training-data versioning. The warning is concrete: “once you remove this, you also want to remove it from your fine-tuning data.” [00:46:58]
- **What needs qualification:** The report recommends learning how to validate model-based judges, saying to compare them with “human judgment.” Here automated grading is future work: “First we're just trying to make this work first.” [00:48:43] The video cannot validate Shreya's involvement, the later course, or a working automated-judge process. There is no direct report error about this video to correct because it was not cited.
- **Additional evidence about regressions:** The report's general iteration advice gains a visible failure tradeoff here: “we actually increase this other error.” [00:59:47] A better result on the targeted issue can hide damage elsewhere.

## Fit for the user's agent workspace

- (inference) Record worker requests, tool calls, results, and final responses together. Attach the instruction version and code commit so a failed run can be reconstructed.
- (inference) Start with observable worker failures and simple checks, such as missing deliverables, malformed output, or work outside the packet's scope. Do not choose a scoring platform before seeing examples.
- (inference) Reuse TypeScript and existing automation if that lowers setup cost. This source offers a concrete reason to avoid requiring a separate Python service.
- (inference) Build a small review view with accept/reject, notes, scenario filters, and links to complete runs. Treat faster human inspection as useful infrastructure.
- (inference) Track failures separately when comparing worker models or instruction changes. A model that fixes one failure may introduce another.
- (inference) Use generated task variations to supplement real worker runs, then retain human review after automated filtering. Passing assertions only removes the failures those assertions detect.
- (inference) Skip fine-tuning and reward-model work initially unless there is a clear need. Copy the inspection and regression loop first. The video does not provide a worker cost/value formula or evidence for autonomous scope judgment.
